**Cobra Gold** (Thai: คอบร้าโกลด์) refers to multi-national [Indo-Pacific](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pacific "Indo-Pacific") [military exercises](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_exercises "Military exercises") held in [Thailand](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"). They are among the largest annual exercises of their kind.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Cobra_Gold_exchange.jpg/250px-Cobra_Gold_exchange.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cobra_Gold_exchange.jpg)

Royal Thai and U.S. military training together during Cobra Gold 2020

Cobra Gold was first held in 1982 in an effort to improve coordination between the armed forces of the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and [Thailand](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") in both hostile military and [humanitarian](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanitarianism "Humanitarianism") efforts.[[1]](#cite_note-ehrlich-1)

As of 2021, Cobra Gold has several different activities that highlight regional security and effective regional crisis responses. The first is the Combined Arms Live-Fire Exercise (CALFEX), in which live ammunition is aimed at predetermined targets as troops advance and close in on their target. A [Command Post Exercise](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_exercise "Military exercise") (CPX) is when military officers engage in computerized war games, disaster relief, or humanitarian missions over several days. An Amphibious Exercise (AMPHIBEX) combines ship-to-shore movement capabilities, with vertical envelopment between the [Royal Thai Armed Forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_Armed_Forces "Royal Thai Armed Forces") and U.S. military, with allied forces dependent on operational developments.

In 2020, Cobra Gold introduced landmine reduction operation and introduced U.S. Marine Corps [F-35B Lightning II fighter aircraft](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_F-35_Lightning_II "Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II") and the [high mobility artillery rocket system (HIMARS)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M142_HIMARS "M142 HIMARS").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Cobra_Gold_AMPHIBEX.jpg/250px-Cobra_Gold_AMPHIBEX.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cobra_Gold_AMPHIBEX.jpg)

U.S. Marines assault the beach as part of the amphibious beach landing at Hat Yao Beach, Thailand, during Cobra Gold 2020

Cobra Gold expanded to include 27 nations as of 2021,[[2]](#cite_note-slavin-2) including [Indonesia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [Malaysia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia"), [Singapore](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore"), [South Korea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), and other [South Asian](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") and Pacific Ocean countries. [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") was admitted to Cobra Gold exercises for the first time in 2015, although Chinese military forces were only allowed to participate in humanitarian assistance training.[[1]](#cite_note-ehrlich-1) Most nations participate in Cobra Gold as observers rather than as participants.[[3]](#cite_note-cronk-3) In 2020, these countries participated in the exercise: [[4]](#cite_note-4)

* Participants: the United States, Thailand, Singapore, South Korea, Indonesia, Japan, and Malaysia
* Observers: Brunei, Laos, Cambodia, Israel, Vietnam, Germany, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Brazil, and Sweden
* Multinational Planning Augmentation Team: Australia, Canada, France, the United Kingdom, Nepal, the Philippines, Fiji, and New Zealand
* Others:[*[clarification needed](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*] China and India.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

## Cobra Gold Exercises 2013–2016

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Cobra_Gold&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Cobra Gold Exercises 2013–2016")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Cobra_Gold_amphibex.jpg/250px-Cobra_Gold_amphibex.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cobra_Gold_amphibex.jpg)

U.S. Marines participate in the amphibious beach landing at Hat Yao Beach, Thailand during Cobra Gold 2020

Participants in Cobra Gold 2013 included the United States, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand. Twenty other nations participated as observers. For the first time, [Burma](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burma "Burma") joined the exercise (as an observer). Activities held during Cobra Gold 2013 included an [amphibious landing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibious_warfare "Amphibious warfare") involving [ground assault fighter jets](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_aircraft "Attack aircraft"), [attack helicopters](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_helicopter "Attack helicopter"), and [landing craft](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landing_craft "Landing craft"); mock military raids involving small boats and helicopters; a practice evacuation involving civilian populations; a [combined arms](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_arms "Combined arms") exercise held while live fire occurred overhead and nearby; and training in [biological](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_warfare "Biological warfare"), [chemical](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_warfare "Chemical warfare"), [jungle](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungle_warfare "Jungle warfare"), [nuclear](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warfare "Nuclear warfare"), and [radiological warfare](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiological_warfare "Radiological warfare").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Admiral [Samuel J. Locklear III](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_J._Locklear "Samuel J. Locklear"), commander of the [United States Pacific Command](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Pacific_Command "United States Pacific Command"), described Cobra Gold as "the Pacific's signature exercise" in 2014 and noted that it was among the largest multinational military exercises in which U.S. armed forces participate.[[3]](#cite_note-cronk-3)

The United States reduced its participation in Cobra Gold 2015 because it disapproved of the military [coup in Thailand](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Thai_coup_d'état "2014 Thai coup d'état") in 2014.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The U.S. sent 3,600 troops to the exercise in 2015, down from 4,300 in 2014. They also canceled the exercise in which troops practiced under live fire during an amphibious landing. However, American military forces participated in a civilian evacuation training exercise and a field training exercise in cooperation with other nations' military forces.[[1]](#cite_note-ehrlich-1) More than 13,000 military personnel from six nations participated in Cobra Gold 2015, while other nations participated as observers.[[2]](#cite_note-slavin-2)

The United States postponed its participation in a March 2015 meeting with Thailand to begin planning for Cobra Gold 2016. American military officials indicated they might cancel the exercise outright as a protest against continuing military rule in Thailand.[[2]](#cite_note-slavin-2)

U.S. Marine assault amphibious vehicles (AAVs) during an amphibious beach landing during Cobra Gold 2020

This marked the 36th anniversary of the Cobra Gold exercise.[[8]](#cite_note-Bangkokpost-8) Cobra Gold 2017 aimed to improve capabilities among participating nations, including conducting joint operations and building relationships.[[9]](#cite_note-Castaneda-9) Also, it aimed to enhance the relationship between Thailand and the United States after the Thai power seizure in 2014 caused Thai-U.S. relations to deteriorate. ## Exercise Cobra Gold 2020

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Cobra_Gold&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Exercise Cobra Gold 2020")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Cobra_Gold_F-35B.jpg/250px-Cobra_Gold_F-35B.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cobra_Gold_F-35B.jpg)

U.S. Marine F-35Bs conducting flight operations during Cobra Gold 2020

Twenty-seven nations participated in the 39th iteration of Cobra Gold, from February 25 to March 6, 2020. Cobra Gold 20 aimed to enhance the capabilities of participating nations to plan and conduct combined and joint operation, build relationships among participating nations across the region, and improve interoperability over a range of activities, including strengthening maritime security, preventing and mitigating emerging disease threats, and responding to large-scale natural disasters.

Cobra Gold 2020 introduced a new landmine reduction operation and the participation of the Marine Corps [F-35B Lightning II](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin_F-35_Lightning_II "Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II") fighter aircraft and [High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M142_HIMARS "M142 HIMARS"). The HIMARS purpose is to conduct bilateral training at the battery-level on the weapon system, developing interoperability between the United States, the [Royal Thai Air Force (RTAF)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_Air_Force "Royal Thai Air Force"), and other regional nations and partners. The continuation of exercises such as Cobra Gold demonstrates the commitment of the Kingdom of Thailand and the United States to their long-standing alliance. [[*according to whom?*](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")]

Leaders and commanders from Indo-Pacific nations participating in Cobra Gold 2020 came together to give final remarks and shake hands as the two-week-long exercise came to a close at [Ban Dan Lan Hoi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_Dan_Lan_Hoi_District "Ban Dan Lan Hoi District"), Kingdom of Thailand on March 6, 2020.

The United States has engaged in only a single, very minor military intervention in the Pacific area since the end of the [Vietnam War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), making it challenging to judge Cobra Gold's effectiveness in improving warfighting capabilities and coordination.[[15]](#cite_note-Hayton-15): 229

Cobra Gold has proven effective in improving coordinated military response to natural disasters, including the [2004 Indian Ocean tsunami](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami "2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami"), the [2011 Tōhoku tsunami](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tōhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami "2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami"), and disaster relief provided to the [Philippines](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") after [Typhoon Haiyan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoon_Haiyan "Typhoon Haiyan") struck in November 2013.[[15]](#cite_note-Hayton-15): 228

Statement from International IDEA — On 7 August 2024, Thailand’s Constitutional Court ruled to disband the Move Forward Party (MFP) and banned its executives including former leader, Pita Limjaroenrat, from standing for elections, setting up a new political party or taking part in forming a new party for 10 years. This decision undermines democratic principles and marks a severe setback for democratic development in the Kingdom of Thailand.

The ruling followed a decision by the Court on 31 January, which stated that MFP’s attempts to amend Section 112 of the Criminal Code, known as the lèse-majesté law, demonstrated an intent to undermine the constitutional monarchy. The MFP defended its actions, clarifying that its intention was not to undermine the monarchy but to propose amendments to an outdated law, including reducing the severe penalties attached to *lèse-majesté* offenses, in line with their election manifesto and following numerous and long-standing recommendations by international human rights bodies and advocacy groups.

In a parliamentary democracy, it is crucial that members of parliament can propose and discuss law reforms without fear of repercussions. The dissolution of the party and the ban on its executives is a disproportionate punishment for such actions.

The dissolution of the MFP in 2024 is just the latest in a series of political parties being disbanded or banned since the military coup of 2006. Thailand’s Constitution of 2017, adopted following the military coup of 2014, continues to facilitate such lawfare and is in dire need of democratic reform.

(*The Move Forward Party won the most seats in the 2023 general election and has remained the most popular party according to opinion polls. The next general election is scheduled for 2027*).

[Commentary](/commentary)

Thailand’s 2023 general election winners are confronted by a gauntlet of obstacles. An alternative coalition comprising of conservative parties could easily form in their place, says this lecturer from Naresuan University.

![Commentary: Thailand’s military machinations will define post-election political manoeuvring](https://dam.mediacorp.sg/image/upload/s--U4hLmwJq--/c_fill,g_auto,h_468,w_830/fl_relative,g_south_east,l_one-cms:core:watermark:reuters,w_0.1/f_auto,q_auto/v1/one-cms/core/2023-06-27t082542z_1_lynxmpej5q08n_rtroptp_3_thailand-election.jpg?itok=Y5UrYyV_ "Commentary: Thailand’s military machinations will define post-election political manoeuvring")


File Photo: Over a month after Pita Limjaroenrat's Move Forward Party won a decisive victory in the country’s general election, a minefield of legal, political and military obstacles is hindering his accession to the premiership. (Photo: Reuters/Athit Perawongmetha)

[![](https://dam.mediacorp.sg/image/upload/s--CTW2x5qB--/c_fill,g_faces:auto,h_140,w_140/f_auto,q_auto/paul-chambers-thumbnail.png?itok=1K4439mi)](/author/paul-chambers)

28 Jun 2023 06:11AM

PHITSANULOK, Thailand: Over a month after Thailand’s [progressive Move Forward Party](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-pita-limjaroenrat-move-forward-election-win-speech-3489871) and its [prime ministerial candidate Pita Limjaroenrat](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-pita-limjaroenrat-election-prime-minister-enough-support-3589016) won a decisive victory in the country’s general election, a minefield of legal, political and military obstacles is hindering his accession to prime minister.

The Election Commission is investigating whether Pita contested the election while [illegally holding media shares](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-election-move-forward-party-pita-limjaroenrat-media-shares-3556306). If found guilty, Pita would be barred from office, Move Forward could be dissolved and its winning MPs might be disqualified.

On June 20, the Election Commission [endorsed all 500 winning electoral candidates](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-election-all-mp-elects-endorsed-election-commission-3572291), though it left open the possibility of investigating any later.

## MOVE FORWARD AND PHEU THAI REMAIN AT ODDS

But the Move Forward-led eight-party, 312-member coalition-in-waiting (which includes Pheu Thai) still needs 64 of the 250-member [junta-appointed Senate](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-general-election-senate-upper-house-pita-limjaroenrat-premiership-3500486) to achieve the constitutionally mandated 376 seats to form government.

Even before parliamentary approval, Move Forward and Pheu Thai remain at loggerheads over which of them will [fill the slot of Lower House speaker](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-move-forward-party-house-speaker-position-change-constitution-3514151). Since only a speaker can nominate a prime minister, their failure to agree could prevent any from being selected.

In fact, Pheu Thai would clearly like to dump Move Forward so that it can lead a coalition of its own. The speaker squabble provides a convenient issue for doing so, though cabinet allocation disagreements or an Election Commission verdict against Pita could also do the trick.

Rumours have spread about secret negotiations to form an alternative coalition between Pheu Thai (141 seats), Bhumjaithai (71 seats) and the Democrats (25 seats). Pheu Thai has publicly refused to form a government with Prayut Chan-o-cha’s 36-seat United Thai Nation Party or Prawit Wongsuwon’s 40-seat Palang Pracharat Party because of their role in the 2014 military coup.

Though it might ignore the vehemently anti-Thaksin Prayut, Pheu Thai may ultimately accept Prawit’s help to obtain the prime minister position.

## BHUMJAITHAI’S ANUTIN CHARNVIRAKUL COULD SEEK TO BE PRIME MINISTER

Depending on how successfully arch-royalist forces manipulate the Senate, it could vote down any potential Pheu Thai prime minister. If that happens, [Bhumjaithai](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/bhumjaithai-party-play-political-kingmaker-after-thailand-may-14-election-coalition-pheu-thai-3481126) and its leader [Anutin Charnvirakul](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/thailand-cannabis-health-minister-anutin-charnvirakul-bhumjaithai-party-election-3412191) could seek the prime minister role.

Anutin would be supported by the five principal arch-royalist parties, comprising 182 seats, and his demonstrated royalism would placate the Senate.

But without Pheu Thai, a prime minister with a minority in the Lower House could easily be censured, unless the Election Commission disqualifies all 151 Move Forward MPs.

Anutin could remain prime minister until Thailand’s arch-royalist Senate loses its powers to vote with the Lower House in selecting prime ministers - constitutionally scheduled to end in May 2024 - but his government would be frail and short-lived.

Alternatively, if a coalition is agreed upon whereby Anutin is the prime ministerial candidate heading a government composed of the larger Pheu Thai, micro-parties and either the Democrats or Prawit’s Palang Pracharat, the Senate would likely affirm Anutin and he could form a long-lasting majority.

If Anutin cannot become prime minister, the parties of Prawit and Prayut will see prime ministerial nominations in that order.

While it is conceivable, though unlikely, that Thailand’s entrenched monarchy and monarchised military would allow Move Forward’s Pita or Pheu Thai’s Srettha Thavisin to become prime minister, such a scenario would likely lead right-wing political opponents to act to bring the coalition down.

This could return Thailand to the years of political pandemonium between 2011 and 2014 that preceded the most recent military coup.

## PRAYUT CHAN-O-CHA COULD SIGN OFF MILITARY RESHUFFLE

Amid the political turbulence, Prayut Chan-o-cha continues as caretaker prime minister. By staying in office, he can influence the forces who might stage a future coup by signing off on the military reshuffle list which prime ministers must give to the king for endorsement each year.

The reshuffle takes effect annually on Oct 1 and Prayut could send a list to the palace at the beginning of August before he steps down.

2023 is extremely significant because it is the first time in at least two decades that all security commanders (including army, navy, air force and police) will be rotated simultaneously. The army is by far the most important service, with the others having a far smaller budget.

Prayut wants to guarantee that arch-royalist military loyalists, especially from powerful pre-cadet classes 23 and 26, take all key army command postings.

In particular, he is seeking to ensure that his personal protégé Deputy Army Commander General Jaroenchai Hintao becomes Army Chief while Deputy Commander of the Royal Thai Armed Forces General Songwit Noonpakdi and First Army Commander General Pana Klaewplodsuk become Commander of the Royal Thai Armed Forces and Deputy Army Commander respectively.

Caretaker Prime Minister Prayut Chan-O-Cha can influence the forces who might stage a future coup by signing off on the military reshuffle list, which prime ministers must give to the king for endorsement each year. (Photo: AFP/Lillian Suwanrumpha)

Prawit-loyalist Assistant Army Chief General Suksan Nongbualuang has a chance to beat out Jaroenchai as Army Commander, after which Pana would succeed him. Should Pita or Srettha become prime minister, they would likely prefer the weaker General Ukrit Boontanonda to be army chief.

But a military selection board, dominated by arch-royalist service chiefs, votes on promotions above the level of general and it is doubtful that Ukrit would get the nod. Moreover, though Pita or Srettha could try to cancel Prayut’s reshuffle, Jaroenchai, as Deputy Army Commander, would simply become the acting chief and only he or Suksan could pass the board.

The leadership of Thailand’s army-dominant military will not be obedient to progressive civilian leaders and look set to oppose any reformist measures by Move Forward or Pheu Thai.

Thailand’s progressive 2023 election winners are confronted by a gauntlet of obstacles. Move Forward and Pheu Thai face cases before the Election Commission and must pass the junta-appointed Senate.

An alternative coalition comprising only conservative parties or Pheu Thai with conservative parties could easily form, especially if the Election Commission disqualifies Move Forward MPs.

If a progressive prime minister takes office, Thailand will likely look forward to growing pandemonium. Meanwhile, caretaker Prime Minister Prayut will use the reshuffle to ensure that the military leadership remains firmly independent of elected civilian control for years to come.

*Dr Paul Chambers is Lecturer at the Centre of ASEAN Community Studies, Naresuan University, Thailand. This commentary [first appeared](https://www.eastasiaforum.org/2023/06/26/thailands-military-machinations-will-define-post-election-political-manoeuvring/) on East Asia Forum.*

The status of national capital is to be officially conferred on Nusantara in Kalimantan by mid-2024.

Given the strategic location, heritage qualities and high value of the properties to be vacated, the ADB urged the government to devise an asset-repurposing strategy that is aligned with livability criteria, which matches people’s economic interests and is financially feasible at the same time.

“It is crucial that we view the relocation to the new capital as an opportunity for making a positive impact to enhance Jakarta for the benefit of all its residents,” Joris van Etten, a principal portfolio management specialist at ADB’s Indonesia Resident Mission, told The Jakarta Post at the 2023 Jakarta Architecture Festival on Friday.

He said the gradual process of Jakarta government buildings being vacated over the next four to five years provided the local government with a window to strategize and optimize the economic benefits for all citizens.

However, he asserted: “This goes beyond simply converting these assets into revenue-generating possibilities; it’s about creating a livable Jakarta.”

The ADB has been assisting the Finance Ministry in planning Jakarta’s asset-repurposing strategy with the aim of improving the city’s livability and maximizing the country’s economic interests, according to a report on the ministry’s website.

The development financier urged the government to forge long-term partnerships with investors and property developers to ensure the sustainable maintenance of these assets.

The total value of government assets in the city amounts to Rp 1.464 quadrillion (US$95.23 billion), comprising land, housing and buildings, according to the ADB.

During the relocation to Nusantara, all ministries and agencies will be mandated to formally transfer their assets, according to the Finance Ministry.

The Finance Ministry’s State Assets Directorate General (DJKN) will be tasked with overseeing and managing these assets in Jakarta once they are vacated, adhering to the principles of “highest and best use”, according to the State Assets Director General Rionald Silaban.

The directorate general is in charge of managing state property, government investment, state debt and receivables.

Though Van Etten did not specify the ideal ratio between public and private investment to maximize economic benefits, he noted: “When it comes to financing, cities are primarily funded by the private sector through real estate development.”

He recommended repurposing the government assets to serve functions including high-class apartments, logistical hubs, data centres, hotels, hospitals and other core living facilities.

Read also: Local investors kick-start commercial projects in Nusantara

At the same event, Jakarta Investment and One-Stop Integrated Service (PTSP) head Benny Agus Chandra pointed out that, despite the state’s ownership of those vacant government buildings, the local government retained the authority to propose and advocate for ways to repurpose and redesign them for the city’s improvement, including for affordable housing initiatives.

“The local government is confident about developing Jakarta. Despite the land ownership held by the ministries, we can assert our authority [to develop the properties],” Benny stated.

He suggested that relocating the nation’s capital offered an opportunity to centralize residential and business zones in Jakarta’s various districts to transform the city into a global business hub.

Benny added that ongoing expansion of the city’s transit system had spurred growth in areas outside the city centre, such as Halim in East Jakarta, an airport and new modes of public transportation like the high-speed rail connecting Jakarta and Bandung, which had, in turn, increased the value of the land.

Iwan Kurniawan, head of the Jakarta Development and Environment Bureau, said the government was currently drafting a law on the Jakarta Special Region, which aimed to secure and facilitate in the city’s future development. The bill included alternative financing methods for future infrastructure projects to reduce reliance on the regional budget.

Iwan added that draft provisions on spatial planning in Jakarta sought to centre business activities and residential settlements around transit hubs, with a residential density target of 70 %.

These transit hubs connect networks operated by the Jakarta MRT, the Greater Jakarta LRT and the Commuter Line that connect the city with its suburbs.

The **Royal Thai Army** or **RTA** ([Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"): กองทัพบกไทย; [RTGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_General_System_of_Transcription "Royal Thai General System of Transcription"): **kong thap bok thai**) is the [army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army "Army") of [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") and the oldest and largest branch of the [Royal Thai Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Thai_Armed_Forces "Royal Thai Armed Forces").

The Royal Thai Army is responsible for protecting the kingdom's sovereignty. The army was formed in 1874, partly as a response to new security threats following the 1855 [Bowring Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowring_Treaty "Bowring Treaty") with [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), which opened the country for international trade.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

In modern era, the army has a long history of [coups d'état and coup attempts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coups_d'%C3%A9tat_and_coup_attempts_by_country#Thailand "List of coups d'état and coup attempts by country"). Its leadership continues to see coup-making as one role of the army.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

On 22 May 2014 the army deposed the government, appointed military officers to the [national assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Thailand "National Assembly of Thailand"), and on 21 August 2014 they elected the army's Commander in Chief, General [Prayut Chan-o-cha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayut_Chan-o-cha "Prayut Chan-o-cha"), as prime minister. The general retired October 2014[[6]](#cite_note-6) to concentrate on political reform which he said would take at least a year, following which he promised national elections would be held.[[7]](#cite_note-ThailandPM-7)

The existence of an information warfare unit participating in a cyber campaign against government critics was leaked to the public in late February 2020.[[8]](#cite_note-8) In 2020 Twitter shut down a network of accounts which were engaged in [information warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_warfare "Information warfare"). According to Twitter "Our investigation uncovered a network of accounts partaking in information operations that we can reliably link to the Royal Thai Army (RTA)."[[9]](#cite_note-9) The operation had targeted the political opposition within Thailand. The Thai Army denied that they had been involved in the disinformation operation.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

One point of comparison: as of 1 November 2019, the [US Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Army "US Army") had 322 general officers[[11]](#cite_note-CRS-44389-11): 2 for a force of 471,990 troops.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Saiyud Kerdphol is Thailand's oldest general, a veteran of World War II and Korea who retired in 1983 as supreme commander. During his tenure, general officer numbers were based on the number of troops under their command. As of 2019, only 150–200 four-star generals occupy command positions. Speaking on the topic of army manpower, Saiyud declared that, "Everybody being a general is unbelievable. Full generals don't have a seat to sit in or a job to do."[[13]](#cite_note-NAR-20191231-13)

The **digital wallet scheme** is a government [handout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handout "Handout") scheme created by the Thai government that aims to allow eligible Thai citizens to receive ฿10,000 (US$275) each through a [digital wallet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_wallet "Digital wallet") to spark economic growth. The scheme is the flagship policy of the [Pheu Thai party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheu_Thai_Party "Pheu Thai Party") and the [Srettha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srettha_Thavisin "Srettha Thavisin") and [Paetongtarn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paetongtarn_Shinawatra "Paetongtarn Shinawatra") governments. The handout of approximately ฿450 billion is estimated to reach 45 million registered people.

The scheme is designed to spark economic growth in Thailand's sluggish [economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Thailand "Economy of Thailand") post-[COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") by increasing the country's [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP"), growth and household [purchasing power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power "Purchasing power") through promoting consumption at the local level amongst lower level income earners.[[2]](#cite_note-:8-2)[[3]](#cite_note-:9-3) It also aims to promote digitisation.[[3]](#cite_note-:9-3) Phase 1 of the scheme was launched on 25 September 2024, with the initial 14.2 million recipients being welfare card holders and the disabled.[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4) It has been criticised by economists who label it as costly and harmful to Thailand's economy.[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5)

## Eligibility and restrictions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Digital_wallet_scheme&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Eligibility and restrictions")]

Recipients must have been at least 16 years old by 30 September 2024 and a Thai citizen to receive the handout. The recipient's yearly income must also have been below ฿840,000 and their bank accounts must have contained less than ฿500,000 by 31 March 2025. The requirement of [bank accounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_account "Bank account") applies to current, savings and fixed-deposit accounts, but not state bank savings lotteries or foreign currency deposits. Recipients must also not be currently serving out a prison sentence or have a prison sentence.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6) Shop owners and people with a record of fraud are also excluded.[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) Out of Thailand's population of around 67 million, the government estimated that about 50 million people were eligible for the scheme, although the Ministry of Finance estimated only 45 million people would register. A total of 36 million individuals registered in the first round.[[7]](#cite_note-:6-7)

After the ฿10,000 was distributed, there was a six-month time limit for spending the funds. The money could not be withdrawn as cash, but people who receive the handout in the first phase also received some of it in cash.[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)[[8]](#cite_note-8) There are also restrictions on where and what the money can be spent on. It can only be spent within the recipient's registered [district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Thailand "Districts of Thailand") and at participating businesses, which excludes major retail stores, wholesale outlets and department stores.[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) Originally, the money could only be spent within a 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) radius around where they lived.[[9]](#cite_note-9) However, an obstacle to this is that a large portion of the eligible population in urban centres like [Bangkok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangkok "Bangkok") and [Chiang Mai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Mai "Chiang Mai") are registered in other [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Thailand "Provinces of Thailand").[[2]](#cite_note-:8-2)

Additionally, the money could not be spent on 18 items, which include [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_beverage "Alcoholic beverage"), [cannabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_in_Thailand "Cannabis in Thailand") products, cash and souvenir vouchers, [diamonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond"), electrical appliances, electronic equipment, fuel oil, [gems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemstone "Gemstone"), [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold"), [kratom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kratom "Kratom") products, [lotteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotteries "Lotteries"), [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas"), [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"), services, or online products. There exists doubt over the government's ability to monitor spending and prevent the purchase of restricted items, although these restrictions are built into the digital wallet.[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5)[[3]](#cite_note-:9-3) An April survey by [Siam Commercial Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siam_Commercial_Bank "Siam Commercial Bank") found around 40% of those surveyed intended to spend it on necessities such as food and health products. In the same survey, over 80% said they would redirect their personal income to make loan payments or invest in businesses while the handout money would be used for what their personal income would have bought.[[2]](#cite_note-:8-2)

The Srettha government has frequently flip-flopped over how the scheme would be financed. The Pheu Thai party had proposed that it be funded through the budgets, but the new coalition government led by Srettha instead proposed a special parliament bill to request one-time borrowing. The bill was met with criticism by the [Bank of Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Thailand "Bank of Thailand"), economists and the opposition [Move Forward party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Move_Forward_Party "Move Forward Party").[[10]](#cite_note-:3-10) The government then sought to have it funded by the [Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Cooperatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_for_Agriculture_and_Agricultural_Co-operatives "Bank for Agriculture and Agricultural Co-operatives") (BAAC).[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5) However, the legality of this was in question as it could violate laws governing government saving banks.[[11]](#cite_note-:4-11)

This was then changed in favour of pulling money out of the governments 2024-2025 fiscal budget. This change was announced on 10 April 2024, where Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin said the scheme would be funded solely by the 2024-2025 fiscal budget. According to the Deputy Finance Minister Julapun Amorvivat, the needed ฿450 billion will be funded by ฿175 billion from the 2024 budget, ฿152.7 billion from the 2025 budget, and ฿172.3 billion from the BAAC's 2025 budget.[[12]](#cite_note-12) The total cost also dropped from ฿500 to ฿450.[[13]](#cite_note-:7-13)

After phase 1 was launched on 25 September, Deputy Finance Minister Paopoom Rojanasakul announced that the government had sufficient funding for phase 2 to go ahead. Phase 1 had used ฿145 billion, with ฿180 billion already allocated to phase 2.[[14]](#cite_note-:5-14)

## Background of the insurgency

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Southern_Thailand_insurgency&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background of the insurgency")]

### Historical background

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Southern_Thailand_insurgency&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Historical background")]

Despite the ethnic affinity of the people of the [Patani region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patani_(historical_region) "Patani (historical region)") with their Malay neighbours to the south, the old [Patani Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patani_Kingdom "Patani Kingdom") was led by [sultans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan "Sultan") who historically preferred to pay tribute to the distant Siamese kings in Bangkok. For many centuries the King of Siam restricted himself to exacting a periodic tribute in the form of [Bunga mas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunga_mas "Bunga mas"), ritual trees with gold leaves and flowers that were a symbolic acknowledgment of Siamese [suzerainty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzerainty "Suzerainty"), leaving the Patani rulers largely alone.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

### Forced assimilation and local nationalism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Southern_Thailand_insurgency&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Forced assimilation and local nationalism")]

Thai rule over the historical Patani region was confirmed by the [Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Siamese_Treaty_of_1909 "Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909"). Until well into the 20th century, the government in Bangkok had interfered little locally, relying on local officials for the implementation of policies within the Patani region. This included an exemption in implementing Thai Civil Law, which had allowed Muslims to continue their observance of local [Islamic laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_law "Islamic law") regarding issues on inheritance and family. However, by 1934 Marshal [Plaek Phibunsongkhram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaek_Phibunsongkhram "Plaek Phibunsongkhram") set in motion of a process of [Thaification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thaification "Thaification") which had as its objective the [cultural assimilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_assimilation "Cultural assimilation") of the Patani people, among other ethnic groups in Thailand.[[59]](#cite_note-59)

The [National Culture Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_cultural_mandates "Thai cultural mandates") was enforced as a result of the Thaification process, promoting the concept of "Thai-ness" and its [centralist aims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralism "Centralism"). Its "Mandate 3" was directly aimed at the Patani people.[[60]](#cite_note-60) By 1944, Thai civil law was enforced throughout the land including the Patani region, over-riding earlier concessions to local Islamic administrative practices.[[61]](#cite_note-61) The school curriculum was revised to be Thai-centric, with all lessons in the [Thai language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_language "Thai language"), to the detriment of the local [Jawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelantan-Pattani_Malay "Kelantan-Pattani Malay"). Traditional Muslim courts that formerly handled civil cases were removed and replaced with civil courts run and approved by the central government in Bangkok. This forced assimilation process and the perceived imposition of Thai-Buddhist cultural practices upon their society were irritants to the ethnic Malay Patani.[[62]](#cite_note-62)

In 1947, [Haji Sulong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haji_Sulong "Haji Sulong"), founder of the [Patani People's Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patani_People's_Movement?action=edit&redlink=1 "Patani People's Movement (page does not exist)"), launched a petition campaign, demanding autonomy, language, and cultural rights, and implementation of Islamic law.[[63]](#cite_note-RAND-63) In January 1948, Sulong was arrested on treason charges along with other local leaders branded as "separatist". Shortly after Sulong's arrest, the [Greater Patani Malay Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Patani_Malay_Association "Greater Patani Malay Association") ([Malay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_language "Malay language"): *Gabungan Melayu Patani Raya*) was founded by [Tengku Mahmood Mahyideen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tengku_Mahmood_Mahyideen "Tengku Mahmood Mahyideen") to advocate for his release. General elections were held in [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") on 14 May 2023 to elect 500 members of the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_(Thailand) "House of Representatives (Thailand)").[[2]](#cite_note-3) The [Move Forward Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Move_Forward_Party "Move Forward Party"), led by [Pita Limjaroenrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pita_Limjaroenrat "Pita Limjaroenrat"), surprised analysts by winning the most seats, followed by fellow opposition party [Pheu Thai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheu_Thai_Party "Pheu Thai Party") who had won the most seats in the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Thai_general_election "2011 Thai general election") and [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Thai_general_election "2019 Thai general election") elections. Turnout was a record 75.22%.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-4)[[4]](#cite_note-5)

The elections were held using a [parallel voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_voting "Parallel voting") system as in the [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_constitution_of_Thailand "1997 constitution of Thailand") and [2007 constitutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_constitution_of_Thailand "2007 constitution of Thailand"), in contrast to the [mixed-member apportionment system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation "Mixed-member proportional representation") used in 2019. Like in 2019, the elected prime minister did not need to be a member of the House and would be chosen by the full [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(Thailand) "National Assembly (Thailand)"), including the 250 military-appointed members of the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Thailand "Senate of Thailand"), for a total 376-seat majority. Due to the structure of the National Assembly, experts had warned of a possible [gridlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gridlock_(politics) "Gridlock (politics)") scenario in which the current opposition parties secure more than half of the House votes but are obstructed in the Senate. Additionally, the Election Commission had received criticism over untrustworthiness, unprofessionalism, and bias in its conducting of the voting process.

Contents of https://www.eastasiaforum.org/2023/06/26/thailands-military-machinations-will-define-post-election-political-manoeuvring/:
The Election Commission (EC) is investigating whether Pita contested the election while illegally holding media shares. If found guilty, Pita would be [barred from office](https://www.matichon.co.th/politics/news_4021825), Move Forward could be dissolved and its winning MPs might be [disqualified](https://www.thaipbsworld.com/the-share-saga-that-threatens-to-end-thai-hopes-for-a-liberal-prime-minister/). On 20 June, the EC endorsed all 500 winning electoral candidates, though it left open the possibility of investigating any later.

But the Move Forward-led eight-party, 312-member coalition-in-waiting — which includes Pheu Thai — still needs 64 of the 250-member junta-appointed Senate to achieve the constitutionally-mandated 376 seats to form [government](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-05-30/thai-coalition-forms-transition-team-as-it-chases-senate-support). Even before parliamentary approval, Move Forward and Pheu Thai remain at loggerheads over which of them will fill the slot of Lower House speaker. Since only a speaker can nominate a prime minister, their failure to agree could prevent any from being selected.

In fact, Pheu Thai would clearly like to dump Move Forward so that it can lead a coalition of its own. The speaker squabble provides a convenient issue for doing so, though cabinet allocation disagreements or an EC verdict against Pita could also do the trick.

Rumours have spread about secret negotiations to form an alternative coalition between Pheu Thai (141 seats), Bhumjai Thai (71 seats) and the [Democrats](https://www.thaiexaminer.com/thai-news-foreigners/2023/06/04/democrat-leader-warns-of-voices-of-hate-topping-spirit-of-democracy/) (25 seats). Pheu Thai has [publicly refused](https://www.nationthailand.com/thailand/politics/40027563) to form government with Prayuth’s 36-seat Ruam Thai Sang Chart party or Prawit’s 40-seat Palang Pracharat party because of their role in the 2014–2019 junta. Though it might ignore the vehemently anti-Thaksin Prayuth, Pheu Thai may ultimately accept Prawit’s help to obtain the premiership.

Depending on how successfully arch-royalist forces manipulate the Senate, it could vote down any potential Pheu Thai prime minister. If that happens, Bhumjai Thai and its leader Anutin Charnvirakul could seek the premiership. Anutin would be supported by the five principal arch-royalist parties, comprising 182 seats, and his demonstrated royalism would placate the Senate.

But without Pheu Thai, a prime minister with a minority in the Lower House could easily be censured, unless the EC disqualifies all 151 Move Forward MPs. Anutin could remain prime minister until Thailand’s arch-royalist Senate loses its powers to vote with the Lower House in selecting prime ministers — constitutionally scheduled to end in May 2024 — but his government would be frail and short-lived.

Alternatively, if a coalition is agreed upon whereby Anutin is the prime ministerial candidate heading a government composed of the larger Pheu Thai, micro-parties and either the Democrats or Prawit’s Palang Pracharat, the Senate would likely affirm Anutin and he could form a long-lasting majority. If Anutin cannot become prime minister, the parties of Prawit and Prayuth will see prime ministerial nominations in that order.

While it is conceivable, though unlikely, that Thailand’s entrenched monarchy and [monarchised military](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00472336.2016.1161060?journalCode=rjoc20) would allow Move Forward’s Pita or Pheu Thai’s Srettha Thavisin to become prime minister, such a scenario would likely lead right-wing political opponents to act to bring the coalition down. This could return Thailand to the years of political pandemonium in 2011–2014 that [preceded the most recent military coup](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-thailand-protest-idUSBREA4J0HN20140523).

Amid the political turbulence, Prayuth Chan-ocha continues as caretaker prime minister. By staying in office, he can influence the forces who [might stage a future coup](https://www.eastasiaforum.org/2023/05/29/after-thai-elections-an-unstoppable-political-force-meets-an-immovable-object/) by signing off on the military reshuffle list which prime ministers must give to the king for endorsement each year.

The reshuffle takes effect annually on 1 October and Prayuth could send a list to the palace at the beginning of August before he steps down. 2023 is extremely significant because it is the first time in at least two decades that all security commanders (including army, navy, air force and police) will be rotated simultaneously. The army is by far the most important service, with the others having a [far smaller budget](https://www.trade.gov/country-commercial-guides/thailand-defense-and-security#:~:text=An%20estimated%2049%20percent%20of,the%20Royal%20Thai%20Air%20Force.). Prayuth wants to guarantee that arch-royalist military loyalists, especially from powerful pre-cadet classes 23 and 26, take all key army command postings.

In particular, he is seeking to ensure that his personal protégé Deputy Army Commander General Jaroenchai Hintao becomes Army Chief while Deputy Commander of the Royal Thai Armed Forces General Songwit Noonpakdi and First Army Commander General Pana Klaewplodsuk become Commander of the Royal Thai Armed Forces and Deputy Army Commander respectively. Prawit-loyalist Assistant Army Chief General Suksan Nongbualuang has a chance to beat out Jaroenchai as Army Commander, after which Pana [would succeed him](https://mgronline.com/crime/detail/9660000012546). Should Pita or Srettha become prime minister, they would likely prefer the weaker General Ukrit Boontanonda to be army chief.

But a military selections board, dominated by arch-royalist service chiefs, votes on promotions above the level of [general](https://www.hsfk.de/fileadmin/HSFK/hsfk_downloads/prif121.pdf) and it is doubtful that Ukrit would get the nod. Moreover, though Pita or Srettha could try to cancel Prayuth’s reshuffle, Jaroenchai, as Deputy Army Commander, would simply become the acting chief and only he or Suksan could pass the board. The leadership of Thailand’s army-dominant military will not be obedient to progressive civilian leaders and look set to oppose any reformist measures by Move Forward or Pheu Thai.

Thailand’s progressive 2023 election winners are [confronted by a gauntlet of obstacles](https://www.eastasiaforum.org/2023/05/28/though-the-thai-elections-done-and-dusted-the-political-uncertainty-remains/). Move Forward and Pheu Thai face cases before the Election Commission and must pass the junta-appointed Senate. An alternative coalition comprising only conservative parties or Pheu Thai with conservative parties could easily form, especially if the Election Commission disqualifies Move Forward MPs. If a progressive prime minister takes office, Thailand will likely look forward to growing pandemonium. Meanwhile, caretaker Prime Minister Prayuth will use the reshuffle to ensure that the military leadership remains firmly independent of elected civilian control for years to come.

*Dr Paul Chambers is Lecturer at the Centre of ASEAN Community Studies, Naresuan University, Thailand, and has published extensively on military affairs in Southeast Asia.*
